newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Analysts give Nestle data mixed reviews.
newsitem.headline: Analysts give Nestle data mixed reviews.

text.p: Financial analysts gave a mostly positive response to news Nestle SA's 1996 group sales rose more than 7.1 percent to 60.5 billion Swiss francs, but some said it should have done even better given the weakening franc.
"This is pretty positive," said Anne Alexander at Credit Suisse First Boston in London, adding it was too early to say whether she would upgrade her "hold" recommendation for the shares.
"This is at the top range of the consensus, just below the 60.6 billion I was expecting."
For the first time since 1993, exchange rates had a positive effect of 1.4 percent, Nestle said, adding volume growth excluding acquisitions and disinvestments was 2.7 percent.

It recorded strong volume growth in the Asia/Pacific region, Africa and the Middle East. Growth was above average in Europe, due primarily to rapid expansion in central and eastern Europe, and in Latin America, but was disappointing in the U.S. market.

"It's good because of central Europe, the emerging markets," Alexander said. "Volume is all right. I suppose pricing must have had a good effect because I was expecting a bit more from currency exchanges."

James Amoroso at Bank Julius Baer said the 60.5 billion figure was higher than the 60.3 billion he had expected, even though volume growth was lower than his 3.1 percent forecast and the currency factor was below his 1.9 percent view.
He was perplexed at how pricing could have made up the difference because the effect of acquisitions was hardly changed from the 0.6 percent seen after 10 months.
The pricing component of growth was 2.4 percent, he said, up from 1.5 percent after 10 months.
Wilhelm Blaeuer at Pictet et Cie in Geneva said Nestle should have been able to exploit the currency factor better to wring more sales from abroad, especially in late 1996.

"I would be happy if the currency effect would be 1.7 or 1.8 percent. I don't mind this. But (it is not good) to be so low in comparison to Roche, which had 2.5 percent. We will see Novartis figures with two-point-something percent since Swiss companies have more or less the same geographically balanced portfolio."

He said the difference could reflect problems Nestle acknowledged it faced in the United States. "It could show they are having real problems in the U.S.," he said. "Maybe that also has an effect on the currency side."

He said 2.7 percent volume growth was below the 3.2 percent he was expecting, adding the decline from 3.6 percent in the first half and from three percent after 10 months was worrying. He played down Nestle's forecast of rising 1997 sales and profit.
"Are they saying something which might induce anybody to upgrade their estimates? I don't think so," Blaeuer said.

"For us it is more or less slightly disappointing, he added. "For the food sector it is still a good figure, maybe not the best figure, but it is not a terrible figure. I simply don't see where the huge potential is for next year and the year after."
